        User: How much storage space on a hard drive is taken up by addresses and names of files?
        Assistant: The short answer is "not much". The longer answer is that there is much more file metadata than just file names and data location, and it depends alot on the particular filesystem that you are using. However, many filesystems will store things like file names in directories, which are treated as special types of files themselves, while most of the actual metadata (file size, ownership, location, etc...) are stored in special areas (such as an "inode") which are set aside when the filesystem is created. The percentage of space that is set aside for this can be configured, so I suppose the answer here is "whatever you want". However a default ratio which I've seen alot for Linux filesystems is 256/16384 (which would be about 1.5% of the disk). Note that I assumed we are talking about filesystem metadata here. If you are talking about higher-level metadata, that would often be found inside files themselves (like image or audio files), then that really just depends on what files you have.

        User: What makes an organism count as a whole new species? Where is the line that says "this isn't a Tyrannosaurus Rex, this is a chicken"?
        Assistant: The distinction between T. Rex and a chicken is pretty clear; morphologically they are very different, and represent two (related but) divergent lineages of evolution. Sometimes it's that easy. But I think your question is more along the lines of "When did Pilohippus become the modern horse?" It's like asking "when does red become blue in this gradient?" Obviously, the ends are pretty clearly different, but a lot of the middle purplish stuff is hard to determine. With this kind of phyletic evolution, were the two organisms on either end somehow able to exist in the same time and place they would be unable to produce offspring. This is one quality that allows us to call them different species. Everything in between is proverbial shades of purple. You've also stumbled into a broad question about species. Taxonomy is a human invention, a way to categorize what we know and see about organisms, but not all organisms fit very neatly into the boxes we've made.

        User: What are the requirements for a planet to he habitable
        Assistant: Right now, basically all that scientists can tell about planets around other stars is two things: how big they are, and how far away from the star they are. Scientists have lately been finding a ton of these planets, and some of them are "potentially habitable" (this is pretty much always what the scientists will call them, not straight up "habitable"). So what potentially habitable means is related to these two things we know about the planets: size and distance. First, it means that the planet is the right size to be habitable (namely, it's not a huge gas giant planet like Jupiter). Second, it means that the planet is neither super close to the star (and therefore way too hot for life) or super far from the star (and an iceball). Now, this doesn't guarantee the planet actually _is_ habitable (Earth, Venus, and Mars would probably all look _potentially_ habitable) but it's really all we can say until we get a chance to find out more about them.
